1	// RUN: %testDafnyForEachResolver "%s" -- --warn-deprecation:false
     2	
     3	
     4	/*
     5	Rustan Leino, 5 Oct 2011
     6	
     7	COST Verification Competition, Challenge 3: Two equal elements
     8	http://foveoos2011.cost-ic0701.org/verification-competition
     9	
    10	Given: An integer array a of length n+2 with n>=2. It is known that at
    11	least two values stored in the array appear twice (i.e., there are at
    12	least two duplets).
    13	
    14	Implement and verify a program finding such two values.
    15	
    16	You may assume that the array contains values between 0 and n-1.
    17	*/
    18	
    19	// Remarks:
    20	
    21	// The implementation of method 'Search' takes one pass through the elements of
    22	// the given array.  To keep track of what it has seen, it allocates an array as
    23	// temporary storage--I imagine that this is what the competition designers
    24	// had in mind, since the problem description says one can assume the values
    25	// of the given array to lie in the range 0..n.
    26	
    27	// To keep track of whether it already has found one duplicate, the method
    28	// sets the output variables p and q as follows:
    29	//   p != q   - no duplicates found yet
    30	//   p == q   - one duplicate found so far, namely the value stored in p and q
    31	// Note, the loop invariant does not need to say anything about the state
    32	// of two duplicates having been found, because when the second duplicate is
    33	// found, the method returns.
    34	
    35	// What needs to be human-trusted about this program is the specification of
    36	// 'Search'.  The specification straightforwardly lists the assumptions stated
    37	// in the problem description, including the given fact that the array contains
    38	// (at least) two distinct elements that each occurs (at least) twice.  To
    39	// trust the specification of 'Search', a human also needs to trust the definition
    40	// of 'IsDuplicate' and its auxiliary function 'IsPrefixDuplicate'.
    41	
    42	// About Dafny:
    43	// As always (when it is successful), Dafny verifies that the program does not
    44	// cause any run-time errors (like array index bounds errors), that the program
    45	// terminates, that expressions and functions are well defined, and that all
    46	// specifications are satisfied.  The language prevents type errors by being type
    47	// safe, prevents dangling pointers by not having an "address-of" or "deallocate"
    48	// operation (which is accommodated at run time by a garbage collector), and
    49	// prevents arithmetic overflow errors by using mathematical integers (which
    50	// is accommodated at run time by using BigNum's).  By proving that programs
    51	// terminate, Dafny proves that a program's time usage is finite, which implies
    52	// that the program's space usage is finite too.  However, executing the
    53	// program may fall short of your hopes if you don't have enough time or
    54	// space; that is, the program may run out of space or may fail to terminate in
    55	// your lifetime, because Dafny does not prove that the time or space needed by
    56	// the program matches your execution environment.  The only input fed to
    57	// the Dafny verifier/compiler is the program text below; Dafny then automatically
    58	// verifies and compiles the program (for this program in less than 11 seconds)
    59	// without further human intervention.
    60	
    61	ghost predicate IsDuplicate(a: array<int>, p: int)
    62	  reads a
    63	{
    64	  IsPrefixDuplicate(a, a.Length, p)
    65	}
    66	
    67	ghost predicate IsPrefixDuplicate(a: array<int>, k: int, p: int)
    68	  requires 0 <= k <= a.Length;
    69	  reads a;
    70	{
    71	  exists i,j :: 0 <= i < j < k && a[i] == a[j] == p
    72	}
    73	
    74	method Search(a: array<int>) returns (p: int, q: int)
    75	  requires 4 <= a.Length;
    76	  requires exists p,q :: p != q && IsDuplicate(a, p) && IsDuplicate(a, q);  // two distinct duplicates exist
    77	  requires forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> -1 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2;  // the elements of "a" in the range [0.. a.Length-2]
    78	  ensures p != q && IsDuplicate(a, p) && IsDuplicate(a, q);
    79	{
    80	  // allocate an array "d" and initialize its elements to -1.
    81	  var d := new int[a.Length-2];
    82	  var i := 0;
    83	  while (i < d.Length)
    84	    invariant 0 <= i <= d.Length && forall j :: 0 <= j < i ==> d[j] == -1;
    85	  {
    86	    d[i], i := -1, i+1;
    87	  }
    88	
    89	  i, p, q := 0, 0, 1;
    90	  while (true)
    91	    invariant 0 <= i < a.Length;
    92	    invariant forall j :: 0 <= j < d.Length ==>
    93	                (d[j] == -1 && forall k :: 0 <= k < i ==> a[k] != j) ||
    94	                (0 <= d[j] < i && a[d[j]] == j);
    95	    invariant p == q ==> IsDuplicate(a, p); //WISH remove the trigger on the next line
    96	    invariant forall k {:trigger old(a[k])} :: 0 <= k < i && IsPrefixDuplicate(a, i, a[k]) ==> p == q == a[k];
    97	    decreases a.Length - i;
    98	  {
    99	    var k := d[a[i]];
   100	    assert k < i;  // note, this assertion is really for human consumption; it is not needed by the verifier, and it does not change the performance of the verifier
   101	    if (k == -1) {
   102	      // a[i] does not exist in a[..i]
   103	      d[a[i]] := i;
   104	    } else {
   105	      // we have encountered a duplicate
   106	      assert a[i] == a[k] && IsDuplicate(a, a[i]);  // note, this assertion is really for human consumption; it is not needed by the verifier, and it does not change the performance of the verifier
   107	      if (p != q) {
   108	        // this is the first duplicate encountered
   109	        p, q := a[i], a[i];
   110	      } else if (p == a[i]) {
   111	        // this is another copy of the same duplicate we have seen before
   112	      } else {
   113	        // this is the second duplicate
   114	        q := a[i];
   115	        return;
   116	      }
   117	    }
   118	    i := i + 1;
   119	  }
   120	}
   121

content.text: The precondition allows -1 values; original is `0 <= a[i]`.

input.command:
cat > diagnosis.json <<'EOF'
{"spec_element": "requires",
 "proof_obligation": "preservation",
 "diagnosis": "The range precondition was weakened to -1 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2, so an element of a may be -1 (counterexample a[3089] = -1). Inside the loop body, d[a[i]] then indexes d at -1, which is out of range. The precondition must state that the elements are in [0, a.Length-2), i.e. 0 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2, as in the problem statement."}
EOF
sed -i 's/==> -1 <= a\[i\] < a.Length - 2;/==> 0 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2;/' program.dfy && sed -n 77p program.dfy && dafny verify program.dfy

content.text:
Dafny now verifies `program.dfy` with no errors: "4 verified, 0 errors".

**What was wrong:** the precondition at line 77 allowed array elements to be as low as `-1` (`-1 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2`). The method uses each element as a position in its scratch array `d`, at line 99 (`d[a[i]]`). If an element is `-1`, that reads `d[-1]`, which is out of range. The counterexample shows exactly this case: `a[3089] = -1`. The problem statement says the values lie between 0 and n−1, so the precondition was wrong, not the method body.

**Fix:** I changed the precondition to `requires forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> 0 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2`. Nothing else in the program changed.

`diagnosis.json` was written before the edit:
- `spec_element`: `requires`
- `proof_obligation`: `preservation`. The failing check is inside the loop body, and the faulty precondition is what allows the bad index there.

The command still exits with code 2. That comes from the "semi-colon is not needed here" style warnings, which were already in the file, and not from verification. Dafny counts them as a compile failure unless you pass `--allow-warnings`.
